report:
## Conclusion

The best available evidence indicates that arthroscopic surgery (debridement, lavage, and/or partial meniscectomy) does **not** meaningfully help knee osteoarthritis and should not be routinely used to treat it.

- Two landmark randomized, placebo-controlled trials found no benefit of arthroscopic debridement/lavage over sham surgery, and no added benefit over physical therapy/medical management for patients with moderate-to-severe knee OA (Moseley et al., NEJM 2002, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259; Kirkley et al., NEJM 2008, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).
- The 2022 Cochrane systematic review, pooling 16 RCTs of arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease (including osteoarthritis and degenerative meniscal tears), concluded that arthroscopic surgery provides **little or no clinically important benefit** in pain or function compared with placebo or non-surgical care, and carries surgical risks (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease).
- Based on this evidence, the UK's NICE guidelines explicitly recommend **against** arthroscopic knee washout/debridement for osteoarthritis, listing it among "do not do" interventions, except in cases of a clear mechanical block or acute traumatic meniscal tear (https://ebi.aomrc.org.uk/interventions/knee-arthroscopy-for-patients-with-osteoarthritis/).
- Some surgeons still argue for a limited role in select patients with mild OA plus a clearly symptomatic meniscal tear, but acknowledge that stronger level-I evidence is lacking to support this niche indication (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4318803/).

**Bottom line:** For typical degenerative knee osteoarthritis, arthroscopy is not an effective treatment and should generally be avoided in favor of exercise, weight management, physical therapy, and, if needed, medication or joint replacement.
